nameStory: The broad yoldia gets its name from its notably wide, oval shell shape compared to other yoldia clams. The genus name "Yoldia" honors a Danish naval officer, but this species earned the "broad" modifier because its shell is distinctly wider and more inflated than its slender relatives.
description: The broad yoldia is a small marine clam that lives buried in muddy ocean bottoms off New England's coast. Its glossy, dark brown to olive-green shell typically reaches about 2-3 inches long and has a distinctive oval, inflated shape. Unlike many clams, it has a smooth, almost mirror-like shell surface that feels slippery when wet. This deep-water dweller is rarely seen alive by beachcombers, but empty shells occasionally wash up on sandy beaches.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly broad and inflated oval shape, much wider than other yoldia clams, with the shell feeling surprisingly thick and heavy for its size

idTips.label: Shell Surface
idTips.description: Glossy, mirror-like finish that feels smooth and slippery when wet, without growth rings or ridges

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to chocolate brown exterior, often with a metallic sheen, while the interior is white with a pearly luster

idTips.label: Hinge Teeth
idTips.description: Rows of tiny, comb-like teeth along the hinge that feel sharp to the touch when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Adults typically 2-3 inches long, feeling surprisingly hefty and solid compared to thin-shelled beach clams

habitat: Lives in deep, muddy ocean bottoms typically 100-1000 feet deep off New England's continental shelf. Prefers areas with fine sediment and cold water temperatures. Empty shells may rarely wash up on exposed ocean beaches after storms, particularly along Cape Cod and Maine's outer coasts.

seasonality.spring: Adults are actively feeding in deep waters, but shells are most likely to wash ashore during spring storm season.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season in deep waters, with very rare chance of finding fresh shells on beaches after major storms.
seasonality.fall: Storm season may bring shells to shore, though they're typically weathered by the time they reach the beach.
seasonality.winter: Most likely season to find shells on beaches due to frequent winter storms churning up deep-water sediments.

funFact: This clam is actually a living fossil - its basic body plan and feeding style using thread-like tentacles to capture food particles hasn't changed in over 400 million years, making it older than dinosaurs and even most trees!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark, oval clams like large blue mussels, but the broad yoldia's perfectly smooth, glossy surface and distinctly inflated oval shape set it apart - remember "broad and glossy" versus the ridged, elongated mussel shells.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "clam," broad yoldias are actually more closely related to primitive mollusks called nut clams and represent an ancient lineage that's quite different from common edible clams like quahogs or steamers.
compareHints: **Note: This identification should be considered tentative as broad yoldia records in New England are extremely rare.** Unlike other yoldia species which tend to be more elongated and compressed, the broad yoldia is distinctly wider and more inflated. It's significantly larger than most other deep-water clams in the yoldia family, and its glossy shell surface is more pronounced than related species.
